hints: Look at the diagram of straight wavefronts meeting a gap that is wider than one wavelength and notice how much the waves spread.
Recall that the amount of diffraction depends on the ratio of wavelength $\lambda$ to gap width $w$, with maximum spreading when $\lambda$ is comparable to $w$.
Use $v = f\lambda$ for the ripple tank to connect a change in frequency to a change in $\lambda$, then compare which listed change makes $\lambda / w$ larger.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: plane water wavefronts are incident on a gap and some spreading into the shadow region is already seen.

State the governing rule: significant diffraction occurs when the wavelength $\lambda$ is comparable in size to the gap width $w$; larger $\lambda / w$ gives more spreading and a better demonstration.
Check amplitude: amplitude controls wave energy and observed brightness, not the geometry of spreading, so changing amplitude does not improve diffraction.

Check frequency and gap width using $v = f\lambda$: at approximately constant wave speed $v$, increasing frequency decreases $\lambda$, and increasing gap width $w$ also decreases $\lambda / w$, so both changes reduce spreading.
Increasing $\lambda$ increases $\lambda / w$ toward order 1, producing wider circular spreading beyond the gap. This is option C.

options.A: Increasing amplitude increases wave energy and brightness in the ripple tank but does not change the amount of spreading at the gap.
options.B: For water waves with speed $v = f\lambda$, increasing $f$ decreases $\lambda$, which makes $\lambda$ smaller compared with the gap and reduces diffraction.
options.C: A larger $\lambda$ makes the wavelength more comparable to the gap width, so the waves spread out more strongly after the gap.
options.D: A wider gap makes the gap width much larger than $\lambda$, so the waves continue more nearly in straight lines with less noticeable spreading.
